summary: The great majority of tokens mean dining (III.1), with diners indexed by l-series endings in the Preterit and sometimes overt l-marked noun phrases. Stem III and l- alone do not establish feeding (III.2).
Sense 1 admits food with b- (PrS 15/82; 94/275), bare food lists (94/273–274, 280) and the cognate meal noun (70/118; 105/14–16; 112/303). These are valency variants, not distinct meanings.
Host locations sə bə ḥaṯno, gabayna/gabayye and comitative ʕam ḥḏoḏe describe where or with whom dining occurs. No lexicalised light-verb phrase is established by these routine meal contexts.

Preterit can locate a completed meal before another event, including future planned arrival in 102/57. Infectum appears in narrative, negation and prospective invitations. MAC NE Interview 2/187 supplies the missing Infectum-wa box in hypothetical meal conditions.
Repeated maḥšamme in 73/37, 88/221 and 100/6 resumes an event; repeated mentions and tokens are not independent example contexts. Forms with maḥəš-/maḥaš- retain the supplied spelling.

No example is added: round 1 already brought Preterit, Infectum and Imperativ sense 1 to five each. The Jan contexts are ordinary dining, so the reader thin-cell proposals do not apply to the cumulative entry.

Maḥšamli answers an invitation with a prior meal, giving a result relevant to refusal. maḥšamlan after temporal məd remains Preterit even when embedded in a description of recurrent fasting; the wider context does not create a Preterit-wa form.
ʕam ḥḏoḏe and gabayye code companions/hosts. They do not by themselves change the diner into a provider of supper or establish an idiom.
In PrS 2/38, are lan nuxroye the l-marked diners (sense 1) or recipients of supper (sense 2)? The German favours serving, but the Turoyo form permits both.
In PrS 7/10, does maḥšamle continue the dervish as diner or switch to Ḥetəm as the host providing supper? The provisional decision favours subject continuity.
Reconcile old prs 14/32 with PrS 6/24 and prs 118/29 with PrS 42/58. No citation replacement is justified without an edition map.
PrS 33/16 omits the supper clause in the supplied German; can its translation be aligned with verse 17? In PrS 33/19, is bi qriṯayo locative or a comitative reference to a villager?
Jan 1.25/1252: clarify the fasting chronology and late-day term čaʕčoʕin in a checked translation. Machine English is internally difficult and is not used as an added example.
Does first-person Preterit Maḥšamli conventionally refuse an invitation, or merely state a completed meal here? No separate refusal sense is proposed.
Jan confirms dining invitations, supper with hosts/family and meals before later prayer or discussion. None supplies the hosting/feeding meaning of sense 2.
